items.stimulus:
The arrangement of letters on most English-language keyboards, known as QWERTY after the first six letters of its top row, dates from the mechanical typewriters of the 1870s. A popular account holds that the layout was designed to slow typists down so that the metal type bars would not jam. Historians of technology now doubt this story. The evidence suggests that the designers were mainly trying to separate letter pairs that were often typed in quick succession, which is not the same as slowing the typist. Whatever its origin, the layout was soon adopted by the leading typewriter manufacturers, and typing schools began training students on it.

Once that happened, a self-reinforcing cycle took hold. Employers wanted typists who could start work immediately, so they bought QWERTY machines. Typists, in turn, learned QWERTY because that was what employers owned. Manufacturers had little reason to offer anything else. Economists call this pattern path dependence: an early, partly accidental choice shapes later options, because the cost of switching rises as more people commit to it. The point is not that the first choice was foolish, but that its survival owes more to its head start than to any proven advantage.

Alternative layouts have been proposed many times. The best known, designed in the 1930s, placed the most common letters on the middle row, where the fingers rest. Its supporters reported large gains in speed, but later reviewers pointed out that several of those trials were run by the layout's own inventor and lacked proper comparison groups. Better-controlled studies have found modest differences at most. This matters for the path-dependence argument. If the alternative were dramatically superior, the persistence of QWERTY would be a striking example of a market locking in an inferior standard. If the difference is small, persistence is easier to explain: few people would pay the cost of relearning for a small reward.

Today the original mechanical reason, whatever it was, no longer applies. Touchscreens have no type bars to jam, yet the virtual keyboards on phones still copy the old arrangement. Users who already know where the letters are would find any change frustrating, at least at first, and device makers have no wish to frustrate their customers. The layout endures, in short, because it is already there.

items.stimulus:
Every autumn, a handful of novels are lifted onto a shortlist, photographed beside a trophy and sold in airport bookshops with a gold sticker on the cover. We are told that literary prizes celebrate excellence and introduce readers to books they would otherwise miss. I believe they do more harm than good.

Consider first what a prize does to the market. In the weeks after a major award is announced, sales of the winning novel can rise many times over, while sales of the other shortlisted titles rise far less and the rest of the year's fiction is barely affected. A prize does not widen readers' attention; it narrows it onto one book. Publishers respond rationally, investing in the kind of novel that judges have rewarded before. The result is a literary culture that slowly comes to resemble the tastes of a few dozen judges.

Second, prizes distort how writers work. A young novelist I know told me she had cut the comic chapters from her manuscript because her agent warned that 'prize juries take seriousness seriously'. One anecdote proves little on its own, but it captures a pressure that many writers describe privately: to write the book that might win rather than the book they want to write.

Defenders of prizes point out that a shortlisting can rescue a small publisher or a debut author from obscurity. This is true, and I do not dismiss it. But for every writer rescued there are dozens whose good books are ignored because readers wait to be told which novel of the year to buy. A prize that selects one winner from thousands of entries is a lottery with a respectable face.

Finally, prizes encourage readers to treat literature as a contest. Novels are not sprinters; there is no finishing line on which they can be fairly compared. To declare one novel 'the best of the year' is to pretend that very different books can be ranked on a single scale.

If we care about reading, we should spend the money now poured into ceremonies on libraries, translation grants and local literary festivals, which spread attention rather than concentrate it.

The teacher later found that one mark had been entered wrongly: the student recorded as scoring 41 had actually scored 14, because the two digits had been swapped. All other marks were correct.
items.question: What is the mean of the corrected marks?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 처음 기록된 합 = 31+35+38+38+40+41+42+44+46+48 = 403. 2) 41이 14로 바뀌면 합은 27 줄어 376. 3) 평균 = 376 ÷ 10 = 37.6. 어림 요령: 한 값이 27 줄면 평균은 2.7 준다(40.3 - 2.7). 오답: B 수정 전 평균이다. C 2.7을 더했다. D 수정 후 중앙값이다. E 최빈값이다. 유형 팁: 값 하나가 바뀌면 전체를 다시 더하지 말고 변화량 ÷ 개수로 평균을 고친다. → 정답 A

items.stimulus:
Blood plasma, the liquid part of blood, is used to make medicines for people with immune disorders, bleeding conditions and severe burns. In many countries, demand for these medicines has grown faster than donations, and a large share of the world's supply now comes from a small number of countries that pay donors. This raises a long-running ethical question: should people be paid for giving plasma?

Opponents make three main arguments. First, they worry that payment exploits people on low incomes, who may donate more often than is good for them because they need the money. Second, they argue that payment changes the meaning of donation: what was a gift to strangers becomes a transaction, and this may weaken the sense of shared responsibility on which voluntary systems depend. Third, some fear that paid donors have a reason to hide illnesses that would disqualify them, making the supply less safe.

Supporters reply that each of these concerns can be addressed without banning payment. Limits on how often a person may donate, together with health checks at every visit, protect donors from harm. Modern testing and processing steps, they say, mean that the safety of plasma medicines no longer depends mainly on donors' honesty. As for the meaning of donation, supporters note that we already pay nurses, doctors and the makers of medicines; it is not obvious why the donor should be the only person in the chain who must work for nothing.

Supporters also make a practical point. Countries that rely only on unpaid donors have generally not collected enough plasma to meet their own needs, and so they import medicines made from plasma collected from paid donors elsewhere. Such countries, supporters argue, are in an awkward position: they object to payment in principle while depending on it in practice.

Neither side denies that donors must be protected. The disagreement is about whether payment, carefully regulated, is compatible with that protection, or whether it inevitably undermines it.

items.stimulus:
In 1974 the American philosopher Robert Nozick asked readers to imagine a machine that could give them any experiences they wanted. A person connected to it would lie motionless in a laboratory while the machine stimulated the brain, producing the vivid sense of composing a symphony, winning a race or exploring a foreign city. From the inside, these experiences would be indistinguishable from real ones. Would you agree to stay connected for the rest of your life?

Most people say they would not, and Nozick took this reaction to tell us something important. If the only thing that mattered to us were how our lives feel from the inside, the machine would be the obvious choice, since it can guarantee better experiences than ordinary life. Our reluctance suggests that we also care about other things: really achieving things rather than only seeming to, developing our own character, and living in a world that exists independently of our wishes.

The thought experiment is usually aimed at hedonism, the view that pleasant experience is the only thing that is good in itself. If hedonism were true, the argument goes, refusing the machine would be a mistake; yet the refusal seems reasonable rather than mistaken.

Critics have questioned whether our reactions are reliable. Some point out that people tend to prefer whatever situation they are already in. When the scenario is reversed, and people are told they have been in a machine all along and may now leave it for a real life they know nothing about, many choose to stay. If so, the original refusal may reflect a bias towards the familiar rather than a deep preference for reality. Others note that people may simply not trust the machine to work as promised, which is a practical worry rather than a judgement about what is valuable.

Defenders of the argument reply that the scenario asks us to set these worries aside. Whether people can actually do so is still debated.

items.stimulus:
In the early 1450s, in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg and his partners began printing with movable metal type. The technique combined several existing ideas, including the screw press already used in making wine and paper, and paper itself, which had reached Europe through the Islamic world centuries earlier. What was new was a system for casting large numbers of identical letters quickly and accurately, together with an oil-based ink that would stick to metal.

The method spread with remarkable speed. Within about fifty years, printing shops had been set up in well over two hundred European towns, and historians estimate that several million printed books, perhaps far more, were produced before 1501. Printers were often skilled workers who had trained in one shop and then moved on to set up their own, carrying the technique with them. Many settled in commercial cities such as Venice, which by the 1490s had more presses than any other city in Europe. These cities offered what a printer needed: money to pay for paper and type before any books were sold, trade routes to carry finished copies to distant buyers, and a population of merchants, lawyers and scholars who wanted to read.

Not every printer prospered. Producing a large book tied up money for months, and printers who misjudged demand were left with unsold stock. Several early printers went bankrupt, and Gutenberg himself appears to have lost control of his workshop after a dispute with an investor. The printers who survived tended to be those who chose their titles carefully, favouring books with a reliable market, such as religious texts, school grammars and legal handbooks.

The spread of printing, then, was not simply the result of a brilliant invention. It depended on networks of skilled workers, on investors willing to take risks, and on towns where enough readers could be found.

By ten o'clock Lina had counted the words she owned. There were eleven of them, and she kept them in her mouth like smooth stones, turning them over so they would not get lost. Hello. Thank you. The teacher, Ms Okafor, spoke slowly to her, the way people speak to someone standing on the far side of a river. Lina nodded at the right moments. Nodding, she had discovered, was a kind of bridge that could hold almost any weight.

At lunch a girl with a green hair clip sat beside her and said something long and bright, ending with a question. Lina felt the question hang in the air between them, waiting. She reached for her stones. None of them fitted.

'Yes,' she said at last, because it was the bravest one.

The girl laughed, not unkindly, and then, to Lina's astonishment, held out half of her orange. Perhaps yes had been the right answer after all. Perhaps, Lina thought, in this country yes meant orange.

In the afternoon they sang a song she did not know, and she moved her lips anyway, a half-second behind, like a shadow learning to walk. When the bell rang she found that she owned a twelfth word. She did not know what it meant yet. But it was hers, and she carried it home without dropping it.

B 32배를 세 번 곱하지 않고 더했다(32 x 3). D 표의 T 값은 P 대비 배수이므로 Q와 비교하려면 32로 나눠야 하는데 그대로 읽었다. 유형 팁: 로그 척도의 배수는 규모 차이를 아는 단위(1.0, 2.0)로 쪼개 곱한다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus: Earthquake magnitude is measured on a logarithmic scale. On the scale used here, an increase of 1.0 in magnitude means that about 32 times as much energy is released, and an increase of 2.0 means that about 1,000 times as much energy is released. The table lists five earthquakes recorded by a fictional seismic network, with the energy each released compared with earthquake P.

table.title: Earthquake magnitude and relative energy released

items.question: In a certain region there are, on average, about 100 earthquakes of magnitude 4.0 for every earthquake of magnitude 6.0. Which one of the following is best supported by this information and the table?

options.text: The one magnitude 6.0 earthquake releases about 10 times as much energy as all the magnitude 4.0 earthquakes together.
The magnitude 4.0 earthquakes together release about 100 times as much energy as the magnitude 6.0 earthquake.
The magnitude 4.0 earthquakes together release about the same total energy as the magnitude 6.0 earthquake.
Small earthquakes release most of the region's total energy.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 규모 4.0 지진 하나의 에너지를 1이라 하면 100개의 합은 100이다. 2) 규모 6.0 지진 하나는 1,000이므로 100개 전체의 약 10배다. 오답: B 개수 100을 곱하면서 규모 6.0 지진의 1,000배를 무시했다. C 개수와 에너지 배수를 같다고 보았다. D 큰 지진 하나가 작은 지진 전체보다 훨씬 많은 에너지를 낸다. 유형 팁: 빈도와 크기가 반대로 움직이는 자료는 '개수 x 1개당 크기'로 총량을 비교한다. → 정답 A

items.stimulus: A management consultant argues: 'Building a company culture is like tending a garden. A gardener cannot make a plant grow by pulling on it; she can only provide good soil, water and light, and remove the weeds. In the same way, a manager cannot order employees to be creative or loyal. She can only create the conditions in which those qualities develop, and remove the practices that choke them.'
items.question: Which one of the following identifies the difference between a garden and a company that most seriously undermines the consultant's analogy?

options.text: Gardens are usually outdoors and change with the seasons, whereas most companies operate inside buildings all year.
Unlike plants, employees can understand what a manager asks of them and can choose to respond to direct requests.
Some gardeners use chemical fertilisers, while others prefer natural methods such as compost and careful weeding.
Companies, like gardens, can fail if they are neglected for long periods.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 유비의 핵심은 식물을 잡아당겨 자라게 할 수 없듯 직원에게도 직접 지시로 창의성·충성을 만들 수 없다는 점이다. 2) 식물과 달리 직원은 요청을 이해하고 스스로 응할 수 있다면, 직접적인 요구가 어느 정도 효과를 낼 수 있으므로 유비가 성립하는 바로 그 지점이 무너진다. 오답: A 실내외 차이는 결론과 관계없는 차이다. C 정원사들 사이의 차이로 두 대상의 비교와 무관하다. D 차이가 아니라 공통점이며 오히려 유비를 지지한다. 유형 팁: 유비를 약화하는 것은 '결론에 쓰인 바로 그 성질'에서의 차이이며, 무관한 차이는 약화하지 못한다. → 정답 B

items.stimulus: Density = mass ÷ volume. A solid object floats in a liquid if its density is less than the liquid's density, and sinks if its density is greater. When an object floats, the fraction of its volume below the surface equals (density of object ÷ density of liquid). Fresh water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³, and a strong salt solution used in a school laboratory has a density of 1.20 g/cm³. Five solid blocks were tested.
items.question: Which block or blocks float in the salt solution but sink in fresh water?

options.text: V and W only
Y only
X only
X and Y only
Z only

items.explanation_ko: 1) 밀도: V 75/125 = 0.60, W 48/64 = 0.75, X 110/100 = 1.10, Y 65/50 = 1.30, Z 180/200 = 0.90 (g/cm³). 2) 민물(1.00)에서는 가라앉고 소금물(1.20)에서는 뜨려면 밀도가 1.00보다 크고 1.20보다 작아야 하므로 X만 해당한다. 오답: A V, W는 두 액체 모두에서 뜬다. B Y는 1.30으로 두 액체 모두에서 가라앉는다. D Y를 포함했다. E Z는 0.90으로 민물에서도 뜬다. 유형 팁: 두 기준값 사이에 들어가는지를 묻는 문항은 모든 밀도를 먼저 구해 수직선에 놓는다. → 정답 C

items.explanation_ko: 1) V의 밀도는 75 ÷ 125 = 0.60 g/cm³. 2) 잠기는 비율 = 0.60 ÷ 1.20 = 0.5. 3) 잠기는 부피 = 0.5 x 125 = 62.5 cm³. 오답: A 민물(1.00)에서 잠기는 부피다. B 민물에 떴을 때 수면 위로 나오는 부피다. D 0.60에 1.20을 곱했다. 유형 팁: 액체가 바뀌면 분모(액체 밀도)를 반드시 바꿔 넣는다. → 정답 C

items.question: A new block is cut from the same wax as block Z, with a volume of 50 cm³. What is its mass?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 같은 밀랍이므로 밀도는 Z와 같은 180 ÷ 200 = 0.90 g/cm³. 2) 질량 = 밀도 x 부피 = 0.90 x 50 = 45 g. 검산: 부피가 200의 1/4이므로 질량도 180의 1/4인 45 g. 오답: A 180을 2로 나눴다(비율 오류). B 부피를 밀도로 나눴다(50 ÷ 0.9). C 밀도를 1로 보았다. 유형 팁: 같은 물질이면 질량은 부피에 비례하므로 비례식으로 바로 풀 수 있다. → 정답 D

items.stimulus:
Dr Imani Sato: We've finished the analysis. The new compound made no difference to wound healing in the mice compared with the control group. I think we should write it up and submit it.
Dr Felix Brandt: Submit a result that shows nothing? Journals rarely accept those, and it would cost us three months we could spend on the follow-up study.
Sato: It doesn't show nothing. It shows that the compound doesn't work at this dose, in this model. If we don't publish, another lab may spend a year repeating the same experiment.
Brandt: Or they'll find something we missed. Our sample was only twenty mice per group. A small effect could have slipped through.
Sato: Then we say so. We report the sample size and the range of effects our data can rule out. That's more useful than silence.
Brandt: I'm not against honesty. I'm worried about our next grant. Reviewers count papers in high-profile journals, not careful reports of things that didn't happen.
Sato: That's exactly the problem. If everyone thinks like that, the published record shows only the experiments that worked, and anyone reading it will overestimate how well treatments perform.
Brandt: Fine, but that's a problem for the whole system, not one we can fix with a single paper.
Sato: Every paper in the system is someone's single paper.
Brandt: All right. Let's post it on a public preprint server this month and decide about a journal after the follow-up.
items.question: Which one of the following best describes Brandt's main reason for hesitating to submit the result to a journal?

options.text: He believes the compound probably does work and that, with only twenty mice per group, their negative result must be wrong.
He thinks that negative results should never be made public, even on a preprint server.
He doubts that Sato analysed the data correctly.
He thinks submitting it would cost time and do little for their careers, given what journals and reviewers reward.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 브란트는 학술지가 이런 결과를 잘 받지 않고 후속 연구에 쓸 석 달이 든다고 하고, 다음 연구비 심사에서 심사위원이 고영향 학술지 논문을 센다고 걱정한다. 2) 그의 주된 망설임은 시간 비용과 경력상 이득이 적다는 점이므로 D가 맞다. 오답: A 표본이 작아 작은 효과를 놓쳤을 가능성을 말했을 뿐 화합물이 효과가 있다거나 결과가 틀렸다고 믿지 않는다. B 마지막에 프리프린트 공개에 동의하므로 지나치다. C 분석 자체를 의심한 적이 없다. 유형 팁: 관점 문항은 화자가 반복하는 걱정(시간, 연구비)을 근거로 '주된' 이유를 고른다. → 정답 D

Health guidelines in the fictional country of Ostria classify adult BMI as follows: under 18.5, underweight; 18.5 to under 25, healthy weight; 25 to under 30, overweight; 30 or more, obese. A rugby team's fitness coach recorded data for five players, including body fat measured as a percentage of body mass.
items.question: What is Amos's BMI?
items.explanation_ko: 1) BMI = 질량 ÷ 키². 2) Amos: 120 ÷ (2.0 x 2.0) = 120 ÷ 4 = 30. 오답: A 키를 제곱하지 않고 나눴다(120 ÷ 2). C 키의 제곱을 곱했다(120 x 4). D 키를 곱했다(120 x 2). 유형 팁: 공식에 제곱이 있으면 대입 전에 제곱값부터 계산해 둔다. → 정답 B

items.explanation_ko: 1) BMI는 질량과 키만으로 계산하므로 근육과 지방을 구별하지 못한다. 2) Amos(BMI 30, 체지방 14%), Bello(BMI 약 25.9, 체지방 12%)는 체지방이 낮은데도 비만·과체중으로 분류되므로, 근육량이 많은 선수에게는 BMI 분류가 높게 나올 수 있다는 C가 자료로 뒷받침된다. 오답: A 측정 오류라고 단정할 근거가 없다. B 다섯 명 자료로 모든 선수를 일반화했다. D Eko는 BMI가 20으로 가장 낮고 체지방도 9%로 가장 낮아 반대 사례다. 유형 팁: 과학적 추론은 공식이 무엇을 반영하고 무엇을 반영하지 못하는지에서 결론을 찾는다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus:
Speaker 1 (Hana Lindqvist, political scientist): Compulsory voting produces parliaments that reflect the whole population, rather than the groups most likely to turn out, such as older and wealthier citizens. When everyone must vote, parties cannot win simply by mobilising their loyal supporters; they have to appeal to the middle. A small fine for not voting is a modest price for a more representative result.

Speaker 2 (Oren Mabuza, civil-liberties lawyer): Voting is a right, and a right includes the freedom not to use it. Forcing people to the polls treats abstention as an offence, when it can be a deliberate statement that no candidate deserves support. Citizens who stay at home are not breaking a duty; they are using a freedom. If turnout is low, the cure is better candidates, not fines.

Speaker 3 (Grace Tolentino, election officer): The debate over principle hides a practical point. Where voting is compulsory, a small share of voters spoil their ballots or choose at random, but in my experience the great majority take the task seriously once they are there. Making voting easier, through weekend elections and postal votes, raises turnout too, though less dramatically.

Speaker 4 (Paulo Rennick, university student): My friends who never read the news would just tick the first name on the list. An uninformed vote is worse than no vote, because it dilutes the choices of those who have taken the time to study the issues. I would rather see fewer voters who know what they are choosing. Turnout is not a goal in itself.
items.question: Speakers 2 and 4 both oppose compulsory voting. Which one of the following best describes how their reasons differ?

options.text: Speaker 2 is concerned about the quality of votes, while Speaker 4 is concerned about the cost of fines.
Speaker 2 thinks turnout is already high enough, while Speaker 4 thinks it is too low.
Speaker 2 objects on the grounds of individual freedom, while Speaker 4 objects that uninformed votes harm the result.
Speaker 2 objects to elections in general, while Speaker 4 objects only to fines.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 화자 2는 투표가 권리이며 권리에는 쓰지 않을 자유도 포함된다는 개인의 자유를 근거로 든다. 2) 화자 4는 정보 없이 던진 표가 공부한 사람들의 선택을 희석한다는 결과의 질을 근거로 든다. 오답: A 투표의 질을 걱정하는 쪽은 화자 4이며 벌금 비용을 걱정한 사람은 없다. B 두 사람 모두 투표율 수준을 판단하지 않았다. D 화자 2는 선거 자체를 반대하지 않는다. 유형 팁: 같은 입장의 두 화자를 비교할 때는 결론이 아니라 근거의 종류(권리 대 결과)를 대비한다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus:
Musical traditions around the world differ enormously, yet certain patterns of pitch turn up again and again. Many unrelated cultures use scales built from five notes, known as pentatonic scales, and the interval between a note and the note with twice its frequency, the octave, is treated as a kind of 'sameness' in most traditions. Why should this be?

One explanation looks to the physics of sound. When a string or a voice produces a note, it also produces fainter tones at whole-number multiples of the main frequency. Two notes whose frequencies form simple ratios, such as 2:1 or 3:2, share many of these extra tones, and listeners tend to hear them as blending smoothly. Scales that are rich in such intervals may therefore be easier to sing in tune and to remember, giving them an advantage as songs are passed from one generation to the next.

A second explanation stresses learning. Children absorb the scales of the music around them long before they can name a note, and adults often find unfamiliar scales strange or even unpleasant. On this view, a scale feels natural mainly because it is familiar, and similarities between traditions may partly reflect centuries of contact through trade and migration.

These explanations need not compete. Physical properties of sound may make some scales easier to learn and pass on, while culture decides which of the many possible options a community actually adopts. Research with communities that have had little exposure to other music is beginning to test how much each factor contributes, and early results suggest that preferences once assumed to be universal vary more than expected.
